newsitem.title: UK: Major says vote for Sinn Fein condones violence.
newsitem.headline: Major says vote for Sinn Fein condones violence.

text.p: Shadowed by tight security, Prime Minister John Major on Monday told voters in Northern Ireland that voting for Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, would be equivalent to condoning guerrilla violence.

Condemning the Irish Republican Army for their campaign of disruption ahead of Thursday's British election, Major urged voters in the province to give support to what he called "genuinely democratic parties."
IRA guerrillas, who last year resumed an armed campaign to oust Britain from the province, have caused chaos in mainland Britain in recent weeks with bombs and bomb hoaxes.

Sinn Fein accuses Major of squandering the potential of a 17-month IRA ceasefire which ended last year by refusing to bring Sinn Fein into talks on resolving decades of conflict in Northern Ireland between majority pro-British Protestants and minority Irish Catholics.
Major told reporters as he swept through a central shopping area of Belfast on MOnday that the elections were being "abused" by both Sinn Fein and the IRA.

"Anyone who votes Sinn Fein in this election is condoning the violence," he said. "We have seen, I hope, that people will cast their votes for the genuinely democratic parties in Northern Ireland and I look forward to them to them doing that on Thursday this week."
Police marksmen stood guard on rooftops and Major was shadowed by a phalanx of plain-clothed security men and Royal Ulster Constabulary officers as he mixed with shoppers.

Major laid the foundations for the best chance of lasting peace in the province for decades with a joint plan with the Irish government, launched in 1993. The IRA announced a ceasefire in August 1994 but broke it in February 1996.

Major is adamant that Sinn Fein will not be invited to the multi-party peace talks until the IRA proves it has abandoned violence for good. This position is supported by the Labour Party which is strongly fancied to win the election.
Major said he was visiting the province to show support for his local candidates and to underscore British government support for the people of the province.
He spoke of the continuing need to provide a peace process that met the needs of all of the province's population and made violence as alien in Northern Ireland as in any other part of Britain.

"Although it is often a slow, grinding, frustrating process, the only way to produce a genuine lasting peace for the people of Northern Ireland is to provide a peace that is accepted by people across opinion in Northern Ireland."
